done.why: I was told I had taken all 150 turns the session allows, mid-wander in the maze, with a knife and a leaflet dropped as markers and no sense yet of its shape.

about: The old white house and its underground, rewritten by someone with a dry, careful voice, and with a new presence threaded through it: a tidy 'Management' that clears crawlways, bars the trap door behind you, puts your lamp back after you die, and pins notes on unfinished passages. It's the classic treasure-hunt, but the Empire is still being built, and someone is minding it.

moments.note: The boards nailed 'by someone in more of a hurry than a carpenter' — first sign the prose had a voice of its own.
Standing in an open field and told I can't see any such thing as the field.
The path winds away 'as though it had somewhere better to be.'
After the sack got a careful sentence, the lunch and garlic inside get 'nothing special.'
The trophy case has 'the patient air of something that expects to be filled.'
The trap door crashes shut and someone bars it — and the sword starts to glow.
The crawlway has been cleared lately, rock stacked neatly, fresh pick marks — something new is going on down here.
The chasm: 'a dark that your lamp does not so much light as annoy.'
The painting, 'hard to look at it for long, and harder to look away.'
The chimney's limit stated plainly and well: 'room for you, a light to climb by and one thing more, and not an inch besides.'
The troll with 'a great many teeth, not all of them his own,' watching me 'the way a cook watches a chicken.'
Beheaded on my first real swing; then the death text mentions 'somebody tidy' put my lamp back.
The east passage is unfinished, with a note: 'Back soon. -- The Management.' The world admits it's under construction.
The maze: identical rooms, blocked directions, and no prose to reward the lingering.
The turn cap landed while I was still lost in the maze, with the Management's thread left dangling.

wished: I wished I could examine the field I was standing in, and the forest path from behind the house — the room descriptions name things the examine verb won't see.
I wished the lunch and the garlic had sentences of their own, since nearly everything else did.
I wished the maze had something to read — a scratch, a mark, a note from the Management — so that a reader had a reason to keep going rather than mapping by dropped knives.
I wished I could have followed the Management: knocked on the barred trap door, waited at the unfinished passage, left a note in reply.
I wished death had cost me less of my inventory, or told me where things had scattered to; I never found the rope, sack, bottle or manual again.

lines.line: boarded across with planks nailed every which way, by someone in more of a hurry than a carpenter. Whatever the owners meant by it, they did not mean visitors.
lines.why: The first line that told me this version had a writer behind it, not just a transcription.

lines.line: Someone has cleared it lately: the fallen rock is stacked neatly along one side, and there are fresh pick marks in the roof.
lines.why: The moment the changed world revealed itself — somebody is working down here, and the story is about them.

lines.line: The chasm drops away from your feet into a dark that your lamp does not so much light as annoy. A pebble kicked over the edge is never heard from again. Neither, by the look of it, was whoever kicked the last one.
lines.why: The best paragraph in the place; three sentences, each one earning the next.

lines.line: done with such tenderness that it is hard to look at it for long, and harder to look away. The signature in the corner is too modest to read.
lines.why: The treasure got a sentence that made me want it for its own sake, not for the case.

lines.line: He is watching you the way a cook watches a chicken.
lines.why: A warning I should have heeded, delivered as a joke, which is the house style.

lines.line: Your belongings, such as they were, have not come with you. They are scattered about the Empire, though somebody tidy has put the lamp back in the living room.
lines.why: 'Somebody tidy' — the first time the unseen caretaker was named, even sideways.

lines.line: The passage to the east has not been finished. A note is pinned to the rock: "Back soon. -- The Management."
lines.why: The world confessing to being a work in progress and making it part of the fiction; I wanted to know who they were more than I wanted any treasure.

lines.line: Whoever made this maze had one idea, and saw it through.
lines.why: The maze's only good line, and it's an apology.

fun.why: The house and the first underground rooms were a pleasure to read room by room; the troll fight and the Management's notes gave it stakes and mystery. The last twenty-five turns in the maze drained some of that.

engagement.why: I examined nearly everything and was rewarded nearly every time, and the thread of the tidy someone barring doors and pinning notes kept pulling me forward. The maze was where attention slipped.

difficulty.why: The house puzzles were gentle and well-hinted (the uneven rug, the chimney's stated limit). The troll beheaded me outright once and fell at once the next time, which felt like dice rather than skill. The maze was hard in the dull way.

interestingness.why: A familiar place made strange by an unseen caretaker: cleared crawlways, barred trap doors, a lamp returned after death, an unfinished passage with a note. That's a real idea, and I only got the edge of it.

prose.why: Consistently dry, specific and funny, with sentences that end a half-beat later than you expect: the chasm, the trophy case, the troll, the sword that has been in worse places. It loses a point for the gaps — 'nothing special' objects inside carefully written containers, unexaminable fields and paths, and a maze with nothing to read.
